name: International Monetary Fund

summary.text: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) is an international financial institution conceived at the July 1944 Bretton Woods conference, with 191 member countries. Each member's quota reflects its size in the world economy and determines its voting power and access to IMF resources. IMF lending is conditional: borrowing governments agree to adjust economic policies, with commitments ranging from fiscal and reserve targets to structural reforms, and funds are typically disbursed in installments tied to those actions.

facts.claim: In the 1980s Latin American debt crisis, which began when Mexico said in August 1982 it could not service its debt, the IMF and other official lenders lent countries enough to pay interest on their bank loans in return for structural reforms and deficit cuts. Many cut infrastructure, health and education spending and froze wages; the decade saw high unemployment and falling per-capita income.

sources.title: Latin American Debt Crisis of the 1980s

facts.claim: In the 1997-98 Asian financial crisis, the IMF-supported programs for Thailand, Indonesia and South Korea called for substantial interest-rate increases to stem currency depreciation, restructuring of financial systems, stronger financial regulation, and opening Asian markets to foreign participants, according to IMF First Deputy Managing Director Stanley Fischer.

sources.title: The Asian Crisis and the Changing Role of the IMF (Stanley Fischer)

facts.claim: A 2016 ESMT Berlin study of Greece's first two bailout programmes (about EUR 216 billion from euro-area lenders and the IMF) found that less than 5% (EUR 9.7 billion) went to the Greek fiscal budget. EUR 86.9 billion went to repaying existing debt (including EUR 9.1 billion to the IMF), EUR 52.3 billion to interest payments, EUR 37.3 billion to recapitalizing Greek banks, and EUR 29.7 billion to incentives for private investors to join the 2012 debt restructuring.

sources.title: Where did the Greek bailout money go? (ESMT White Paper WP-16-02)
Most of Greek bailout money went to banks: study

facts.claim: Thailand: on August 20, 1997 the IMF Executive Board approved support for Thailand of up to about US$4 billion over 34 months as part of a bilateral and multilateral package totalling US$17.2 billion; Thailand drew US$14.1 billion before saying it would not use the remaining balances.
facts.quote: the Executive Board approved support of up to about US$4 billion on August 20, 1997, over 34 months. The total package of bilateral and multilateral assistance to Thailand came to US$17.2 billion

sources.title: Recovery from the Asian Crisis and the Role of the IMF, IMF Issues Brief

facts.claim: Indonesia: on November 5, 1997 the IMF approved a three-year stand-by credit for Indonesia of up to SDR 7.338 billion (about US$10.14 billion), 490% of quota, with SDR 2.2 billion available immediately and later drawings tied to quarterly performance targets and reviews. The Congressional Research Service put the overall support package announced that day at about US$40 billion (another CRS report gives US$42.3 billion), including US$4.5 billion from the World Bank and a US$3 billion U.S. secondary line of credit. In August 1998 the undrawn balance was converted into an Extended Arrangement.
facts.quote: The stand-by credit authorized drawings of up to SDR 7.338 billion (about US$10.14 billion) to support Indonesia's macroeconomic stabilization and structural reform program

facts.claim: Korea: on December 4, 1997 the IMF Executive Board approved financing for Korea of up to SDR 15.5 billion (about US$21 billion) over three years. The Congressional Research Service put the total international package at about US$58.2 billion (US$57 billion in another CRS report); the IMF share was therefore roughly a third of the headline figure.

facts.claim: Thailand suspended 58 finance companies on June 27 and August 5, 1997 and required each to submit a rehabilitation plan. The Financial Sector Restructuring Authority (FRA), created under emergency decrees alongside an Asset Management Corporation, reviewed the plans and oversaw closures; in December 1997 the FRA and Ministry of Finance announced the closure of 56 of the 58, which the Washington Post reported on December 8, 1997 as a step mandated by the IMF under the US$17.2 billion bailout. The two survivors reopened; the FRA later auctioned the closed companies' assets, selling core loans with a face value of 584 billion baht for 147 billion baht, about 25 percent.
facts.quote: a step mandated by the International Monetary Fund under terms of a $17.2 billion international bailout ... FRA and MOF announced the closure of 56 of 58 finance companies, giving a clear indication of government resolve

facts.claim: Korea's December 3, 1997 letter of intent described the crisis as stemming from an unprecedented number of highly leveraged conglomerates (chaebols) moving into bankruptcy, with financial institutions having priced risk poorly and financed an excessively large share of corporate investment, resulting in high leverage.
facts.quote: unprecedented number of highly leveraged conglomerates (chaebols) moving into bankruptcy ... financial institutions had priced risks poorly and were willing to finance an excessively large portion of corporate investment plans, resulting in high leveraging

sources.title: Korea Letter of Intent, December 3, 1997

facts.claim: Korea's December 1997 stand-by arrangement committed the government to: placing troubled banks under finance-ministry control with rehabilitation plans due in 30 days and licence revocation if not approved; an exit strategy including closures and mergers and acquisitions by domestic and foreign institutions; approving foreign purchases of domestic bank stakes above the 4% limit where they strengthen the sector, with legislation to align equity-purchase rules with OECD practice; replacing blanket guarantees with limited deposit insurance; and measures to reduce corporations' high debt-to-equity ratios and develop capital markets so that banks finance less of corporate investment.
facts.quote: the supervisory authority would approve foreign purchases of domestic bank stakes above the 4 percent limit where they strengthen the sector, and that legislation would be sent to the National Assembly to align equity-purchase rules with OECD practice

sources.title: Republic of Korea: IMF Stand-By Arrangement, December 5, 1997

facts.claim: An IMF staff working paper on Korea's 1997 crisis records that full foreign ownership of merchant banks was allowed from December 1997, that raising foreign ownership and management of banks was seen as a way to recapitalize them, boost competition and improve management, and that cross-guarantees among chaebol affiliates and growth-over-profit strategies had driven unviable investment; it argues that ending widespread cross-guarantees and wider use of consolidated financial statements would have made lending risk easier to see. The December 1997 programme documents commit Korea to reducing corporate leverage and improving transparency; none of them requires that chaebol groups be broken up.
facts.quote: Starting in December 1997, full foreign ownership of merchant banks has been allowed

sources.title: The Korean Financial Crisis of 1997: A Strategy of Financial Sector Reform
Republic of Korea: IMF Stand-By Arrangement, December 5, 1997

facts.claim: On July 20, 1998 the IMF Executive Board approved financing for Russia totalling SDR 8.5 billion (about US$11.2 billion): an augmentation of Russia's extended arrangement by SDR 6.3 billion (about US$8.3 billion), of which SDR 4.0 billion (about US$5.3 billion) under the Supplemental Reserve Facility, plus SDR 2.16 billion (about US$2.9 billion) under the Compensatory and Contingency Financing Facility; the Fund activated the General Arrangements to Borrow to finance it.
facts.quote: IMF Approves Augmentation of Russia Extended Arrangement and Credit under CCFF; Activates GAB

sources.title: Press Release No. 98/31: IMF Approves Augmentation of Russia Extended Arrangement and Credit under CCFF; Activates GAB

facts.claim: The first drawing under the IMF's July 1998 package for Russia, scheduled for July 20, 1998, was SDR 3.6 billion after the IMF reduced it by SDR 600 million (about US$800 million) because of delays in implementing certain prior actions; later drawings were tied to completion of the eighth and subsequent reviews under the extended arrangement.
facts.quote: the first disbursement has been reduced by SDR 600 million (about US$800 million), in light of delays in implementing certain prior actions

sources.title: Press Release No. 98/31: IMF Approves Augmentation of Russia Extended Arrangement and Credit under CCFF; Activates GAB

facts.claim: At an IMF press briefing on July 13, 1998, First Deputy Managing Director Stanley Fischer described the package then planned for Russia as US$11.2 billion (SDR 8.4 billion) from the IMF, of which US$8.4 billion would be provided from the General Arrangements to Borrow, with US$5.6 billion to be made available on the Executive Board's approval.
facts.quote: $5.6 billion will be made available on the passage of the Board's agreement

sources.title: Press Briefing on Russia, Stanley Fischer (transcript)

facts.claim: On August 17, 1998 the Russian government announced measures that included widening the ruble's exchange-rate band to a corridor of 6 to 9.5 rubles per dollar, a restructuring of ruble-denominated government debt, and temporary limits on capital payments abroad. In a statement issued on August 25, 1998, reprinted in the IMF Survey, Managing Director Michel Camdessus said that confidence in financial markets had not been re-established and that as a result Russia had continued to lose reserves.
facts.quote: On August 17, the Russian government announced a set of measures designed to bolster confidence in the areas of financial and budget policy. These included a widening of the exchange rate band for the ruble

sources.title: IMF Survey, August 31, 1998 (Camdessus statement on Russia)

facts.claim: The IMF's institutional history of the period (James Boughton, Tearing Down Walls, chapter 7) records that before Russia's August 17, 1998 announcement, Camdessus received telephone calls from U.S. Treasury officials Lawrence Summers and Robert Rubin urging him to take a public stand in favor of a default; not knowing that President Yeltsin had already decided on that course, he declined, saying the Fund could not be a party to a non-market solution, and when Russia went ahead with the default on Monday, August 17, he issued a press release that was muted in its support.
facts.quote: When Russia went ahead with the default on Monday, he issued a press release that was pointedly muted in its support.

sources.title: Russia: From Rebirth to Crisis to Recovery, chapter 7 of Tearing Down Walls: The International Monetary Fund 1990-1999
Tearing Down Walls, chapter 7 (PDF)

facts.claim: IMF accounts describe Russia's August 17, 1998 measures as a de facto devaluation of the ruble (an upward shift and widening of the exchange-rate band), a unilateral restructuring of ruble-denominated government debt falling due between August 19, 1998 and December 31, 1999, and a three-month moratorium on the repayment of private external debt including forward contracts; one IMF account puts the affected GKO/OFZ debt at about Rub 190 billion, of which over Rub 80 billion was held by nonresidents.
facts.quote: a unilateral restructuring of ruble-denominated government debt falling due between August 19, 1998 and December 31, 1999

sources.title: Russia: From Rebirth to Crisis to Recovery, chapter 7 of Tearing Down Walls: The International Monetary Fund 1990-1999
Tearing Down Walls, chapter 7 (PDF)
Debt Crisis in Russia: The Road from Default to Sustainability, chapter 7 of Russia Rebounds

facts.claim: At a press conference on August 28, 1998, Camdessus said the IMF regarded Russia's August 17 action as highly regrettable and extremely unfortunate; that the Fund had supported a needed change in Russia's exchange-rate policy but had made every effort to persuade the Russian authorities to avoid a unilateral restructuring of the debt; and that the IMF did not regard that approach as a constructive one for any other country to follow.
facts.quote: the IMF regards the Russian action as highly regrettable and extremely unfortunate; the IMF did support it, a needed change in the exchange policy of Russia, but it's true that we made every effort to try to convince the Russian authorities to avoid the unilateral avenue for restructuring the debt

sources.title: Press Conference of IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus (transcript)

facts.claim: In August 1999 the IMF posted three PricewaterhouseCoopers reports: on relations between the Central Bank of Russia and Financial Management Company Limited (FIMACO), a Jersey company; on the use of the funds the IMF transferred to the Central Bank in July 1998 between July 1 and September 1, 1998; and on the statistics the Central Bank compiled for the IMF from January 1, 1996 to September 1, 1998. The IMF says the reports were made available with the consent of PwC and the Central Bank of Russia; the first was posted on August 5, 1999 and the other two on August 17, 1999, and all three were removed on September 30, 1999 at PwC's request.
facts.quote: PricewaterhouseCoopers reports on relations between the Central Bank of Russia and the Financial Management Company Limited (FIMACO), on the use of funds transferred to the Central Bank by the IMF in July 1998, and on statistics compiled by the Central Bank for the IMF

sources.title: PricewaterhouseCoopers reports on relations between the Central Bank of Russia and FIMACO, on the use of funds transferred to the Central Bank by the IMF in July 1998, and on statistics compiled by the Central Bank for the IMF (index page)

facts.claim: When the IMF Executive Board approved a new stand-by credit for Russia on July 28, 1999, it took note of the audit finding that the July 1998 tranche from the Fund had not been misappropriated, and expressed strong disapproval of the finding that the Central Bank's channelling of domestic transactions through FIMACO and, in 1996, the transfer of assets on the Central Bank's books to FIMACO had given a misleading impression of the true state of Russia's reserves and of monetary and exchange-rate policy.
facts.quote: Directors took note of the findings that the July 1998 tranche from the Fund had not been misappropriated. [...] Directors expressed strong disapproval of the finding that the channeling by the Central Bank of domestic transactions through FIMACO and, in 1996, the transfer of assets in the books of the Central Bank to FIMACO meant that the balance sheet of the Central Bank had given a misleading impression of the true state of reserves and monetary and exchange rate policies.

sources.title: Press Release No. 99/35: IMF Approves Stand-By Credit for Russia
IMF Survey, August 2, 1999 (stand-by credit for Russia)

facts.claim: In a September 1999 note, 'Facts About IMF Lending to Russia', the IMF said the PwC report on FIMACO had uncovered past incidents of misreporting by the Central Bank of Russia to the Fund of the true position of Russia's international reserves and other monetary aggregates.
facts.quote: the report on FIMACO uncovered past incidents of misreporting by the CBR to the Fund of the true position of Russia's international reserves and other monetary aggregates

sources.title: Facts About IMF Lending to Russia

facts.claim: At the IMF's September 9, 1999 press conference on its 1999 Annual Report, the Fund said the audit had been able to track the money the IMF paid into the Russian central bank's account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, from the New York Fed to the commercial bank where the central bank held its money, and from that bank into the foreign-exchange market for intervention in Russia; it added that another audit was under way to make sure money had not been going through other subsidiaries of the central bank.
facts.quote: The audit has been able to track the money that was paid by the IMF into the Russian central bank's account at the New York Fed, from the New York Fed to the commercial bank in which the central bank held its money, and from that bank into the foreign exchange markets for intervention in Russia.

sources.title: Transcript of a Press Conference on the 1999 Annual Report of the IMF

facts.claim: An IMF working paper by John Odling-Smee, 'The IMF and Russia in the 1990s' (WP/04/155, 2004), says of the story that IMF money lent to Russia had been stolen that there was no truth to it, that the documents purporting to prove it were forged, and that a detailed audit of the central bank's accounts followed.
facts.quote: no truth to this: the documents purporting to prove it were forged

openQuestions: Korea's later letters of intent (December 24, 1997; February 7, 1998 and after) carry the corporate-governance commitments (cross-guarantees, consolidated statements, debt-to-equity targets). Their text was not retrieved in this session (search budget ran out); the facts above record the December 3, 1997 letter and the stand-by arrangement only. The 'main bank' and 200% debt-to-equity target details seen only in an encyclopedia summary were left out.

Indonesia package totals differ between CRS reports (US$40 billion vs US$42.3 billion) and other accounts (US$18-23 billion of first-line financing); the IMF's own share (SDR 7.338 billion) is the firm figure.

Russia 1998, the 'first tranche of about $4.8 billion': the IMF's July 20, 1998 release gives the first drawing as SDR 3.6 billion after a SDR 600 million (about US$800 million) cut and does not state a dollar figure for it. Fischer's July 13 figure of US$5.6 billion less the US$800 million cut, or SDR 3.6 billion at the release's implied rate (SDR 8.5 billion = US$11.2 billion), gives about US$4.7-4.8 billion; that dollar figure is arithmetic, not an IMF statement.

IMF News Brief No. 98/30, 'Camdessus Comments on Russian Actions' (August 17, 1998), is cited in the IMF's history but its text was not among the pages returned; the August 25, 1998 statement (IMF Survey, August 31, 1998) and the August 28, 1998 press conference are cited instead. The 'muted in its support' characterisation is the IMF historian's (Boughton), not the news brief's text.

Who commissioned the 1999 PricewaterhouseCoopers reports (the IMF, the Central Bank of Russia, or both) is not stated in the pages returned; the IMF's index says only that they were made available with the consent of PwC and the central bank and were removed on September 30, 1999 at PwC's request. The PwC report texts themselves are no longer on imf.org. The size of the July 28, 1999 stand-by credit was not captured.

The speaker at the September 9, 1999 press conference on the 1999 Annual Report is not identified in the passage returned (the search summary attributed it to the Managing Director); confirm against the transcript. The IMF's institutional history (Boughton) is used for the Summers/Rubin telephone calls and the description of the August 17 measures; the quoted passage was returned by the search tool and should be checked against the chapter.

The IMF's own record (PR 99/35; 'Facts About IMF Lending to Russia'; Odling-Smee 2004) says the July 1998 tranche was not misappropriated and that the FIMACO finding concerned misreporting of reserves, not theft. No non-IMF account of the audit (U.S. congressional hearings of 1999, the PwC reports, or press investigations) was opened, so the site's framing should be tested against those before any claim that IMF money was diverted.

The description of the August 17, 1998 measures (ruble debt falling due August 19, 1998 to December 31, 1999; three-month moratorium on private external debt; about Rub 190 billion of GKO/OFZ debt, over Rub 80 billion held by nonresidents) was returned by the search tool without a single IMF document being identified; Boughton's history chapter and Russia Rebounds chapter 7 are both cited and the passage should be matched to one of them.
